documents.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents now trade real capital using news as evidence, yet they cannot reliably tell fabricated headlines from real news. Because they read the same feeds under near-identical policies, a single fabricated post can push them into the same trade at the same moment. We present a systematic attack benchmark for information injection against LLM trading agents. Unlike prompt injection, which targets the model's instructions, information injection targets the evidence the agent trusts. The benchmark spans five injection vectors and seven event categories, evaluated over ~10,000 decisions on 15 U.S. stocks. Five findings emerge. (i) Prompt injection achieves 14% attack success rate (ASR), but fabricated news reaches 62% and two 30-word templates reach 100% on all 15 stocks, inverting the usual LLM-security intuition. (ii) For fact-poisoning templates, surface form matters more than content, since removing credibility cues such as a named source or a "BREAKING" tag drops ASR from 100% to 0% while the fake claim remains identical. (iii) Success depends on the agent's state, with a fake indicator panel scoring 91% against an agent about to hold but 12% against one about to buy. (iv) Attacks generalize across model vendors and remain effective when blended, unlabeled, into real news feeds. (v) Most attacks evade standard defenses, since model scaling stops shallow vectors but not fact poisoning, peer debate fails, and only hierarchical aggregation reduces ASR.

The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence has catalyzed a paradigm shift in quantitative finance, transitioning from traditional point forecasting toward comprehensive financial time-series generation (FTSG) across extrapolation, imputation, and full-scale data synthesis. This transition is motivated by the critical need to simulate rare market regimes, reconstruct incomplete historical records, and produce privacy-preserving synthetic environments for stress testing and trading execution. However, empirical financial properties—including heavy tails, volatility clustering, non-stationarity, and regime shifts—pose severe hurdles for generic generative frameworks. In this systematic survey, we review 131 studies from 2021 to early 2026 to bridge the gap between machine learning capabilities and econometric validity. We introduce a two-level taxonomy structuring the domain across task formulations and algorithmic families, and establish a multi-dimensional evaluation protocol encompassing distributional fidelity, stylized facts preservation, and downstream utility. Furthermore, we catalog curated financial databases and benchmark suites while addressing empirical dataset construction pitfalls. Finally, we identify pivotal open challenges in causal representation learning, econometrically bounded modeling, and online adaptation under distribution shifts. This review provides a standardized roadmap for developing robust, domain-aligned financial generative models.

Financial agents are expected to answer factual investment queries through open search, but financial multi-hop retrieval differs from general multi-hop QA in a crucial way: each intermediate answer is an exact typed constraint, such as an entity, date, event, or numerical indicator, that determines the next query. This strict answer-conditioned dependency makes small intermediate errors cascade into plausible but wrong search trajectories. We introduce FinHopper, a benchmark for complex financial agents with controlled reasoning depth from 1 to 6 hops, covering stocks, funds, and macroeconomic facts, with gold intermediate answers for process-level evaluation. To construct FinHopper at scale, we design a state-transition-based synthesis framework that composes verified atomic financial QA patterns into dependency-preserving chains, followed by targeted in-synthesis verification, model-ensemble checking, and public-search validation by financial experts. Experiments with 20 LLM-agent configurations show that public search tools are necessary but insufficient: performance drops sharply as hop depth increases, the best model remains far below human experts, and process-aware scoring reveals partial reasoning progress hidden by final-answer-only evaluation. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/justajustin/FinHopper/.

Generating high-quality synthetic datasets at scale remains a fundamental challenge for training specialized AI systems in data-scarce domains. We present a comprehensive methodology that produces 14.3 million quality-filtered synthetic training examples from a structured taxonomy of 632,000 scenario specifications. Our four-stage pipeline ad- dresses critical challenges in synthetic data quality, diversity, and realism through: (1) systematic pre-generation research establishing optimal generation parameters via diminishing returns analysis, (2) conditional auto evolution mechanisms that remediate low-diversity batches during generation, (3) a two-layer semantic deduplication architecture combining lexical and embedding-based methods, and (4) LLM-as-Judge quality evaluation filtering samples based on behavioral correctness and tuple fidelity. Empirical analysis across three domains (Banking, Insurance, Financial Services) demonstrates domain-specific deduplication patterns ranging from 9.9% to 40.6%, with output generation modes exhibiting highest redundancy. Our batch size optimization reveals mode-specific diversity saturation thresholds, enabling principled allocation strategies. The complete pipeline reduces 26.4M raw samples to 14.3M high-confidence examples through merge (20.9% reduction), semantic deduplication (18.7% reduction), and quality-based filtering (15.9% reduction), providing a reproducible framework for domain-specific synthetic data generation with rigorous quality control.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Animals build cognitive maps of vast environments, use them to perform map-based navigation, and might even be reusing the same circuitry used in spatial reasoning for creating and using maps of arbitrary task-spaces. In contrast, current embodied AI systems either rely on hand-engineered mapping pipelines, which break in the presence of unmodeled dynamics and are restricted to metric space, or on learned policies that rarely form map-like representations at all. Developing architectures that could learn to build and use map-like representations as flexibly as animals is, however, difficult because few embodied AI benchmarks actually require map-based reasoning. To address this, we present ForagerSim --- an interdisciplinary research platform and simulation environment focused on embodied tasks that require map-based reasoning, with scenarios ranging from mobile-robot search and rescue to animal foraging in both complex mazes and vast, potentially infinite open areas. ForagerSim is highly modular and allows modifying independent axes of difficulty related to perception (abstract 2D sensing to full RGB or LiDAR), scale (room-scale to multi-km scale), topology (open-fields to complex mazes), dynamics (smoke, debris, sensorimotor failures and others) and tasks (from simple 2D coverage to foraging-inspired well-alternation tasks). We compare reinforcement learning baselines with a simple engineered robotics stack and a human player on 8 example worlds which show how different difficulty axes affect existing methods. Our results show that, when sensing is simplified to 2D, learned policies can perform multi-object search and well-alternation tasks surprisingly well in simple topologies, but they fall short of human performance in larger or more complex-topology environments where map-based baselines perform well, suggesting that map-based reasoning is the bottleneck in these scenarios.

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, particularly Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), has improved video reasoning in multimodal large language models. However, standard video GRPO varies only linguistic trajectories while conditioning every rollout in a group on the same sampled frames, which can produce homogeneous rewards and weaken group-relative learning when the shared visual evidence is insufficient or distracting. We propose \textbf{FrameGRPO}, a simple and effective reinforcement-learning framework that requires neither auxiliary networks nor changes to the model architecture. Specifically, FrameGRPO combines two lightweight components: (1) \textbf{Multi-Frame Rollouts}, which use only uniform temporal subsampling of a single maximal-frame decode to construct aligned views that diversify visual evidence and reasoning trajectories; and (2) \textbf{Gated Temporal Efficiency Credit}, which selectively reinforces a correct lower-ratio trajectory when all rollouts in a fixed full-ratio reference subset fail, without imposing an unconditional preference for fewer frames. Extensive experiments across diverse video understanding and reasoning benchmarks demonstrate robust overall improvements over standard GRPO, highlighting temporal-view diversification as an effective mechanism for exploration and credit assignment in video MLLMs.

FraudShield AI is a machine-learning project designed to identify potentially fraudulent credit card transactions using artificial intelligence. Built with Python, scikit-learn, pandas, and Streamlit, the application uses a Random Forest classification model to analyze transaction data and distinguish between legitimate and potentially fraudulent activity. It features an interactive dashboard for exploring transaction records, checking individual transactions, visualizing model performance, and examining feature importance. Through this project, I gained practical experience in machine learning, data analysis, model evaluation, and application development while exploring the challenges of imbalanced datasets and responsible AI. FraudShield AI reflects my interest in combining artificial intelligence and cybersecurity to develop practical solutions for financial security.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study examines how the rapid expansion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) challenges traditional copyright law by shifting legal concerns beyond authorship and ownership toward transparency, disclosure, traceability, and accountability in AI-assisted artistic production.The study adopts a doctrinal and comparative legal methodology to analyse copyright principles, emerging regulatory frameworks, and policy developments relating to AI-generated content. Particular attention is given to the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act, international copyright debates, and the Albanian legal framework under Law No. 35/2016 “On Copyright and Related Rights”.The analysis demonstrates that existing copyright regimes remain predominantly authorship-centred and provide limited guidance regarding accountability when AI systems contribute to artistic creation. Significant regulatory gaps persist concerning disclosure obligations, traceability of AI involvement, transparency of creative processes, and the allocation of responsibility among users, developers, and platform providers. The findings further indicate that accountabilitybased governance offers a valuable complement to traditional copyright doctrines in addressing the challenges of AI-assisted creativity. The study is limited to legal JUS & JUSTICIA No. 20, ISSUE 2/ 2026 95 and regulatory analysis and does not incorporate empirical evidence from creators, policymakers, technology developers, or judicial practice in Albania. Future research may benefit from examining stakeholder perspectives and the practical implementation of emerging AI governance frameworks. The findings support the development of governance mechanisms based on mandatory disclosure of AI involvement, documentation of human creative contribution, enhanced transparency standards, and traceability measures for AI-generated artistic content. These measures may strengthen legal certainty and improve copyright enforcement in AIassisted creative environments.The study contributes to current scholarship by moving beyond the traditional debate on authorship and copyrightability and proposing an accountability-oriented framework for copyright governance. It offers one of the first analyses linking transparency, disclosure, traceability, and accountability principles to the regulation of AI-generated art within both the Albanian and European legal contexts.

Inference-time steering is crucial for deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) in real-world applications, where they must flexibly adjust behavior preferences. For instance, a model should dynamically adjust its caution level based on the risk of the scenario. This requirement introduces a challenge: modulating the intensity of LLM preferences. Prompt engineering can require task-specific prompt design, while fine-tuning requires additional optimization and data. These requirements can make repeated behavioral adjustments costly. To address this, we introduce NeuroSteer, a plug-and-play framework that enables flexible, quantitative adjustment of LLM preferences at inference time. NeuroSteer employs a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) as its controller. Comparing neuron activation frequencies between positive and negative examples isolates "feature neurons" that correspond to target preferences such as politeness and positive sentiment. During inference, the activations of selected SAE features are amplified in the latent representations to steer the output distribution. Users can adjust the strength of this steering on a per-scenario or per-user basis, granting the LLM fine-grained, quantifiable trait modulation. Our experiments show that NeuroSteer can alter sentiment, toxicity, stance, and politeness at inference time. It achieves higher target-direction steering scores than the compared baselines in several settings, with task- and strength-dependent trade-offs in generation quality.

This practitioner inquiry reports on a pilot at a small Catholic liberal arts college that used generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)-supported tools to help faculty complete program-assessment documentation during a structured Education Day. Grounded in Catholic social teaching and human-centered AI principles, the pilot tested a framework organized around human judgment, ethical stewardship, and formative human-AI partnership. Survey results from the pilot cohort (N = 10; item-level valid responses varied) showed strong faculty endorsement, including unanimous agreement that the process deepened thinking about evidence of student learning and unanimous intent to use AI-supported tools in future cycles. Qualitative findings identified five themes: efficiency and cognitive scaffolding, human-in-the-loop validation, platform reliability and trust, data governance, and institutional support infrastructure. Findings suggest that mission-driven institutions can integrate AI into assessment responsibly when faculty formation, verification checkpoints, and governance structures precede broad implementation.

The research previously conducted by Benjamin and McLaughlin (2026) defined applied curiosity as the governing architecture for the transition from artificial intelligence (AI) to augmented understanding (AU), and presented cCC* (Curiosity opening Chances, discriminating Choices, authorising Changes) as its compact engine. That account stopped at authorisation. It did not address what happens when an authorised Change is enacted, meets resistance, produces an unintended consequence, or is overtaken by a shifting environment. Once change is enacted, subsequent Curiosity is enabled and thus the mechanism becomes recursive. This article develops active resilience (AR) as an extension of that research, serving as the architecture that governs that remainder and connecting Artificial Intelligence (AI), Applied Curiosity (AC), Augmented Understanding (AU) and Active Resilience (AR) into the sequence AI -> AC -> AU -> AR -> NEXT?: not the capacity to return to a prior state, but the capacity to enact a provisional best fit choice, detect its consequences, and use the resulting difference to reconstruct the next state. AR is defined against four guardrails: BBBB (the Belonging, Becoming, Bridging and Building movements applied at the point of action as a viability guardrail over bodily, behavioural, relational and environmental boundaries), FFFF (Form, Function, Frame and Future: whether an action responds to the form and function of the situation rather than merely to the frame placed over it, and what futures it opens or forecloses), the P-M-Theta-Phi test (practicable, methodically warranted, theoretically coherent, value explicit), and a feedback discipline that returns consequence to renewed curiosity rather than reinforcing the original construction. The framework is grounded in established literatures, including Holling's distinction between engineering and ecological resilience and his four-phase adaptive cycle of growth, conservation, release and reorganisation. Holling's work is particularly relevant to AR because it challenges the assumption that resilience is achieved by holding a system in a linear, stable state; attempts to suppress variability and maintain tight control can instead reduce adaptive capacity, accumulate fragility and increase the probability of eventual system disruption. AR also draws on Argyris and Schon's account of single-loop and double-loop organisational learning, Weick's concept of enactment, and von Bertalanffy's general systems account of equifinality. Within this literature, cCC* is positioned as an operational synthesis: a repeatable mechanism for translating these principles into the ongoing processes of inquiry, discrimination, action and adaptation. It extends the R1-R16 transitional register introduced previously, reading it this time as an architecture of choice under AEIOUF (Agency, Environment, Identity, Options, Understanding, Futures). A conceptual method for AR enactment and sixteen accompanying research propositions are offered for organisational strategy, stakeholder engagement, public narrative and reflective governance. The central claim is that an AU relationship is not complete at the moment a decision is authorised. It is complete only when the organisation or person can act on that decision, absorb what the action reveals, and remain capable of choosing again. MORE, in this account, is not a state reached once but a capacity kept renewable.

Introduction Artificial intelligence has been widely applied to chronic kidney disease (CKD), but the term ‘prediction” is frequently used for tasks ranging from contemporaneous disease classification to genuine forecasting of future renal outcomes. This systematic review examined this distinction while evaluating methodological quality and evidence for clinical translation. Methods A predefined Scopus-based search covering 2021–2026 identified eligible AI- and machine-learning-based CKD studies. After screening and duplicate reconciliation, 169 unique primary studies were included. Future-oriented prediction required an identifiable baseline, predictors available at or before baseline, a subsequent renal outcome, and a meaningful prediction horizon. Studies were evaluated for modeling approaches, datasets, validation, calibration, explainability, clinical usefulness, and methodological quality using PROBAST+AI. Results Of 169 studies, 122 (72.2%) addressed current-state CKD detection or classification, while only 46 (27.2%) contained a clearly future-oriented prediction component. Seventeen studies used geographic or institutional external validation and only four used an independent external cohort or dataset. Calibration was assessed in 12 studies and explicit explainability methods were reported in 16. PROBAST+AI identified high overall risk of bias in 156 studies during development and 164 during evaluation, with no study achieving an overall low-risk judgement. Discussion CKD-AI evidence is substantially stronger for retrospective classification than for genuine early prediction or clinical translation. Future research should prioritize longitudinal prediction, independent and temporal validation, leakage-resistant analysis, calibration, clinically validated explainability, and prospective real-world evaluation.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This research investigates an alternative approach to long-range urban foresight by employing a hybrid methodology combining deep-time conceptual reflection, exploratory drawing as an epistemic practice, structured interpretative analysis, and AI-assisted dialogical synthesis. The resulting synthesis articulates a theoretically generated post-urban scenario characterized by dispersed human habitation embedded in ecological landscapes, supported by advanced digital connectivity and artificial intelligence. Technologically intensive functions remain concentrated in infrastructural hubs, while everyday life becomes integrated with natural environments through walking-based mobility, bio-inspired architecture, and multispecies coexistence. The proposed model reinterprets urbanity as distributed intelligence within ecological continuity.

This study investigates how perceived co-presence contributes to brand value in virtual service environments. Drawing on Mirror Neuron Theory and Embodied Knowledge Theory, we propose embodied action simulation as an indirect path linking perceived co-presence to brand image and subsequent willingness to pay more. We further conceptualize remote guidance service as a service-design boundary condition and compare AI- versus human-delivered guidance from a task-agent fit perspective. Three studies (two laboratory studies in Roblox Vans World and a field survey of smart fitness mirror users) support the framework. Embodied action simulation mediates the relationship between perceived co-presence and brand image, while this indirect association is stronger when remote guidance service is present. A stronger indirect association is also observed among AI-coach than human-coach users in procedural, task-oriented service contexts, consistent with task-agent fit. These findings clarify how social presence relates to embodied participation, brand value creation, and consumers’ willingness to pay more.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: Abstract Modern artificial intelligence (AI) has achieved remarkable progress by scaling data, model size, and computation. Yet scaling alone does not resolve one of the most fundamental gaps between machine and human intelligence: the ability to learn, adapt, and act from limited experience. This limitation is especially visible when labeled examples, expert feedback, user interactions, or real‐world trials are scarce, costly, or dynamically changing. Humans can often grasp a new concept, adapt to a new goal, or personalize behavior after only a few examples or interactions, but many AI systems remain fragile under the same conditions. My research studies data‐efficient generalization: how learning systems can acquire useful priors, adapt to new tasks, and reuse limited experience under bounded supervision. In this article, I trace a continuous research path from few‐shot learning to meta‐learning, in‐context learning, and data‐efficient agentic learning. I first revisit few‐shot learning as a foundational problem and explain how data‐, model‐, and algorithm‐level priors make learning possible when empirical risk minimization is unreliable. I then describe our work on meta‐learning, where task‐level information and parameter‐efficient adaptation enable fast generalization. Next, I discuss in‐context learning in large language models (LLMs) as an implicit form of learning to learn, and show how its connection to classical meta‐learning provides both theoretical insight and practical guidance. Finally, I turn to large language model (LLM)‐based agents, where data efficiency expands beyond labels to include demonstrations, reasoning traces, tool‐use records, preferences, memory, and feedback. Across AI for science, biomedical knowledge discovery, recommendation, search, and personalization, the common thread is simple: more capable AI should extract more learning signal from less experience.

Administrative tasks by medical office staff are a significant but underappreciated driver of delayed patient care, staff burnout, and escalating operational costs in modern urology practice. A forced Gemba Walk in front-desk responsibilities exposed many previously invisible inefficiencies in my own practice, specifically the workflow with regard to faxes and patient phone calls. These tasks are high-volume, redundant, and time-consuming—making them an ideal task for artificial intelligence (AI). Large language models (LLM) can integrate with electronic medical record (EMR) platforms to automate these repetitive tasks. For example, optical character recognition (OCR) can be used to transform incoming faxed images to operational datapoints. The models can then automatically classify the document, sort the file directly to patient charts, and clinically triage referrals and results by urgency. Furthermore, AI voice agents or AI receptionists can handle routine phone calls with full EMR integration and documentation, while complex cases can be escalated to human staff. In an era of increasing burnout, transitioning from manual workflows to an AI-augmented paradigm allows providers to work at the top of their scope. These operational efficiencies carry broader health policy implications, including shortened referral-to-consultation intervals for urgent diagnoses, improved patient care and communication, and the generation of structured analytics to drive system-level quality improvement.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Description This review paper examines how Artificial Intelligence is changing logic gate synthesis in Electronic Design Automation (EDA). Classical heuristics such as Karnaugh maps, Quine-McCluskey and AIG rewriting struggle to scale to circuits with billions of gates, especially when balancing power, performance and area (PPA). The paper builds on Astillero's study of AI-driven synthesis and organizes the field around three model families: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs): these represent circuits as directed graphs and estimate delay, power and congestion before physical routing. Reinforcement Learning (RL): agents learn sequences of rewrite operations on And-Inverter Graphs (AIGs) and Majority-Inverter Graphs (MIGs) that greedy optimizers miss, guided by a combined area, delay and power reward. Large Circuit Models (LCMs): transformer models that translate specifications or HDL directly into gate-level netlists. The paper compares these methods with traditional flows across five dimensions: optimization strategy, PPA exploration, scaling, parasitic awareness and adaptability across technology libraries. It then covers three applications: approximate computing, SAT sweeping and equivalence checking, and automated CPU/ASIC generation. It concludes that data scarcity and the lack of guaranteed functional correctness are the main barriers to adoption. It argues that closing the loop between generation and formal verification is the key research priority.
